title: Commentarius In LXXV Psalmos [Attributus]
author: Rufinus Aquileiensis
source: Translated by Claude from tmp392.tmp392.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: 2. Verba mea auribus percipe, Domine, intellige clamorem meum. Vocata Ecclesia (Ex Augustino) in- vocat Deum, ut (co opitulante) pertranseat nequitiam saeculi hujus, et ad cum perveniat. Quae autem sunt aures divinitatis, nisi pietas ejus ei misericordia, quibus nos audire dignatur? Ipsius quoque est intel- ligere clamorem nostrum, attendere et approbare nostri cordis desiderium.
passages.english: 2. Give ear to my words, Lord, understand my cry. The Church, having been called (from Augustine), calls upon God, so that with his help she may pass through the wickedness of this world and come to him. And what are the ears of the Godhead but his kindness and mercy, by which he deigns to hear us? It is his also to understand our cry, to attend to and approve the desire of our heart.
passages.notes: "ad cum" read as "ad eum"; "ei misericordia" read as "et misericordia"; "co opitulante" read as "eo opitulante".

passages.original: 3. Quoniam ad te orabo, Domine, Et protinus ad- jungit, Mane exaudies vocem meam, etc. Quid est quod (Ex Augustino) superius dixit Exaudi, quasi in prae- senti se exaudiri cuperet : nunc vero dicit, Mane exaudies, non exaudi : et. Ad te orabo, et, Adsta- bo, et Videbo? Forte superior ejus oratio ipsam a vocationem ostendit.
passages.english: 3. For to you I will pray, Lord. And he immediately adds, In the morning you will hear my voice, etc. Why is it (from Augustine) that above he said Hear, as though he wished to be heard in the present, but now says, In the morning you will hear, not hear; and, I will pray to you, and, I will stand by, and, I will see? Perhaps his earlier prayer shows the calling itself.
passages.notes: "a vocationem" read as "vocationem"; the stray "a" is likely a footnote mark. "et." after "exaudi" read as "et".

passages.original: 7.), quia ab omnipotente Domino inhabita- tur. Ideo templum appellatur (2. Paral. 18.), quia ab ipso Domino consecratur. Vel templum ideo voca- tur, quia in eo continue caelesti Domino laudes re- feruntur (Psal. 67.). Ait ergo, Adorabo ad templum sanctum tuum in timore. Quia (Ex Augustino) non ait in templo, sed ad templum, intelligendum est non de perfectione, sed de profectu ad perfectionem esse dictum. El fortasse ideo addidit, in timore tuo : quia principium sapientiae timor Domini (Psal.
passages.english: 7.), because it is inhabited by the almighty Lord. It is called a temple (2 Chron. 18) because it is consecrated by the Lord himself. Or it is called a temple because in it praises are continually offered to the heavenly Lord (Ps. 67). So he says, I will worship toward your holy temple in fear. Because (from Augustine) he does not say in the temple but toward the temple, it must be understood as said not of perfection but of progress toward perfection. And perhaps he added in your fear for this reason: because the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Ps.
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence: "[The holy Church is called a house (Matt.] 7)". "El" read as "Et".

passages.original: 7. Quapropter (Ex Augustino) contexit dicens : Laboravi in gemitu meo. Et tanquam parum profue- rit, addit et dicit. Lavabo per singulas noctes lec- tum meum. Lectus est hoc loco appellatus, ubi re- quiescit animus aeger et infirmus, id est, in vo- luptate corporis et delectatione saeculari.
passages.english: 7. Therefore (from Augustine) he continues, saying: I have labored in my groaning. And as though this had availed little, he adds and says: Every night I will wash my bed. Here the bed means that place where the sick and weak mind rests, that is, in bodily pleasure and worldly delight.

passages.original: Id est, merito negligentiae meae persoquentibus inimicis, corruam vacuus a fructu justitiae. Justum est enim, ut ab inimicis victus deci- dat, quisquis se contra eos armis virtutum et bono- rum operum minime roborat. Et bene (Ex Augustino) non ait, si reddidi facientibus mala : sed retribuenti- bus mihi mala. Qui enim retribuit, jam aliquid acce- pit. Majoris autem patientiae est, nec ei mala repen- dere, qui acceptis beneficiis reddit mala pro bonis, quam si nullo ante accepto beneficio nocere voluis- set.
passages.english: That is, with enemies pursuing me as my negligence deserves, may I fall empty of the fruit of righteousness. For it is just that whoever does not strengthen himself against them with the arms of the virtues and of good works should be conquered by his enemies and fall. And well (from Augustine) he does not say, if I repaid those doing evil, but those repaying me evil. For one who repays has already received something. And it is a mark of greater patience not to pay back evil even to one who, having received kindnesses, returns evil for good, than [it would be] if he had wished to harm without having received any kindness before.
passages.notes: "persoquentibus" read as "persequentibus".

passages.original: 18. Et quia (Ex Augustino) hanc perfectus iste jam evaserat, laudat Deum, et dicit : Confitebor Do- mino secundum justitiam ejus, et psallam nomini Do- mini altissimi. Confessio justitiae Dei est, qua ita lo- quimur, Vere Deus justus es, quando et justos sic protegis, ut per teipsum eos illumines, et peccatores sic ordines, ut non tua, sed sua malitia puniantur.
passages.english: 18. And because (from Augustine) this perfect man had already escaped this, he praises God and says: I will confess to the Lord according to his justice, and sing psalms to the name of the Lord most high. The confession of God's justice is that by which we speak thus: Truly, God, you are just, since you so protect the just that you enlighten them through yourself, and so order sinners that they are punished not by your malice but by their own.
passages.notes: The antecedent of "hanc" (feminine) lies in the preceding text, not given.

passages.original: 1. Canitur iste psalmus Pro occultis filii. Et quia noc dicit cujus, intelligendus unigenitus Filius Dei est. Nam et ipse Dominus (Ex Augustino) cum sine additamento ponit Filium, seipsum unigenitum Filium vult intelligi, ubi ait, Si vos Filius liberaverit, tunc vere liberi eritis (Joan. 8.). Non enim dixit Filius Dei, sed tantum dicendo Filius, dat intelligi cujus sit Filius.
passages.english: 1. This psalm is sung For the hidden things of the son. And since it does not say whose, it is to be understood as the only-begotten Son of God. For the Lord himself too (from Augustine), when he puts Son without addition, wishes himself to be understood as the only-begotten Son, where he says, If the Son sets you free, then you will be truly free (John 8). For he did not say Son of God, but by saying only Son he gives to understand whose Son he is.
passages.notes: "noc" read as "non".

passages.original: 12. Psallite Domino qui habitat in Sion, annunciate inter gentes studia ejus. Psalmus quippe dictus est, ubi fit consonantia vocis cum organo. Et in psalmo duo intelligimus : vocem laudis, et consonantiam ope- ris. Ille vero veraciter psallit, qui sic Deum laudat, ut recte vivat. Ipse autem (Ex Augustino) Dominus habitat in Sion (quod interpretatur speculatio) et ge- stat a imaginem Ecclesiae, quae nunc est : sicut Jeru- salem gestat imaginem Ecclesiae quae futura est (Ga- lat. 4.), idest civitatis sanctorum jam angelica vita fruentium : quia Jerusalem interpretatur visio pacis.
passages.english: 12. Sing psalms to the Lord who dwells in Zion, proclaim his doings among the nations. A psalm is so called where there is harmony of voice with instrument. And in a psalm we understand two things: the voice of praise and the harmony of action. He truly sings psalms who so praises God that he lives rightly. And the Lord himself (from Augustine) dwells in Zion (which is interpreted 'watching') and it bears the image of the Church that now is, just as Jerusalem bears the image of the Church that is to come (Gal. 4), that is, of the city of the saints already enjoying the angelic life: for Jerusalem is interpreted 'vision of peace'.
passages.notes: Stray "a" before "imaginem" omitted as a footnote mark. "studia" rendered "doings".

passages.original: 14. Quis est iste clamor pauperum, quem Deus non obliviscitur? sequitur et dicitur : Miserere mei, Domine, vide humilitatem meam de inimi(??)is meis. Quare ergo (Ex Augustino) non dixit, miserere nostri, Domine, ei vide humilitatem nostram de inimicis no- stris? Non tanquam multi pauperes clamant, sed tan- quam unus. An quia unus nunc interpellat pro san- ctis, qui primus pauper pro nobis factus est, cum esset dives (2.
passages.english: 14. What is this cry of the poor which God does not forget? It follows and is said: Have mercy on me, Lord, see my humiliation from my enemies. Why then (from Augustine) did he not say, have mercy on us, Lord, and see our humiliation from our enemies? Not as though many poor cry out, but as one. Is it because one now intercedes for the saints, who first became poor for us when he was rich (2
passages.notes: Sentence continues into the next passage (2 Cor. 8).

passages.original: 28. In laqueo suo humiliabit eum, inclinabit se, et cadet, cum dominatus fuerit pauperum. Laqueus (Ex Augustino) significat insidias : et bene ait, In laqueo suo humiliabit eum : cum enim signa illa lacere cepe- rit, quanto mirabiliora videbuntur hominibus, tanto illi sancti, qui tunc erunt, contemnentur, et quasi p(??)o nihilo habebuntur.
passages.english: 28. In his snare he will humble him; he will bow down and fall when he has lorded it over the poor. The snare (from Augustine) signifies ambushes; and well he says, In his snare he will humble him: for when he begins to work those signs, the more wonderful they seem to men, the more those saints who will be then will be despised and held as nothing.
passages.notes: "lacere cepe- rit" read as "facere coeperit"; "p(??)o nihilo" read as "pro nihilo".

passages.original: Ad illud tempus videtur prospicere, quo non erat d(??)x neque propheta in Israel : et unusquisque quod bonum erat in oculis suis, faciebat (Dan. 3.). Unde in Osee dicitur : Diebus multis sedebunt fil(??)i Israel une rege, sine principe, sine sacrificio, sine altari, sine sacerdotio, sine manifestationibus (Osee 3.). Quod autem ait, Diminutoe sunt veritates, non ideo ait (Ex Augustino), quod veritates diversae sint, quoniam veritus una est, qua illustrantur animaae san- ctae. Sed quoniam multae sunt animae, in ipsis multae veritates dici possunt : sicut ab una facie multae in speculis imagines apparent.
passages.english: He seems to look ahead to that time when there was no leader or prophet in Israel, and each one did what was good in his own eyes (Dan. 3). Hence it is said in Hosea: For many days the children of Israel will sit without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without altar, without priesthood, without manifestations (Hos. 3). But when he says, Truths are diminished, he does not say it (from Augustine) because truths are diverse, since truth is one, by which holy souls are illumined. But because souls are many, many truths can be spoken of in them, just as from one face many images appear in mirrors.
passages.notes: The citation 'Dan. 3' is wrong; the quoted words are from Judges (17:6; 21:24). 'une rege' read as 'sine rege'. 'd(??)x' read as 'dux'.

passages.original: 7. De cujus luce eloquentiae subjunctum est : Eloquia Domini, eloquia casta : argentum igne exami- natum, probatum terroe, purgatum septulum. Casta dicit (Ex Augustino) sine corruptione simulationis. Mul(??)i enim praedicant veritatem non caste, quia vendunt ill(??)m pretio commoditatum hujus saeculis De talibus dicit Apostolus, quoniam Christum annun- ciarent non caste (Philip. 1.). Bene autem argento igne examinato comparantur, quia sicut argentum examinatur igne, ut purum et clarum sit : i(??)a nimi- rum divina eloquia ig(??)e Sancti Spiritus sunt exami- nata. Unde ipse Dominus ait, Verba quae ego loquor vobis, spiritus et vita sunt (Joan. 14.). Et idem Psalmista al(??)bi dixit, Ignitum eloquium tuum vehe- menter (Psal. 118.). Recte autem probatum terrae dicitur : quia divinum eloquium a fidelibus sanctae Ecclesiae rectum et verum esse comprobatur. Quod purgatum est septuplum, per timorem Dei, per pieta- tem, per scientiam, per fortitudinem, per consilium, per intellectum, per sapientiam (Isai.
passages.english: 7. Concerning the light of his eloquence it is added: The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire, proved of the earth, purified sevenfold. He calls them pure (from Augustine) [meaning] without the corruption of pretence. For many preach the truth not purely, because they sell it for the price of the advantages of this world. Of such the Apostle says that they proclaimed Christ not purely (Phil. 1). And they are well compared to silver tried by fire, because just as silver is tried by fire so that it may be pure and bright, so indeed the divine words have been tried by the fire of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Lord himself says, The words that I speak to you are spirit and life (John 14). And the same Psalmist said elsewhere, Your word is exceedingly fiery (Ps. 118). And it is rightly said to be proved of the earth, because the divine word is proved to be right and true by the faithful of holy Church. That it is purified sevenfold [is] through the fear of God, through piety, through knowledge, through fortitude, through counsel, through understanding, through wisdom (Isa.
passages.notes: 'septulum' read as 'septuplum'. The passage breaks off mid-citation (Isa. 11). The quotation 'spirit and life' is actually John 6:63, not John 14.

passages.original: 2. Usquequo, Domine, oblivisceris mein finem? usque– quo avertis faciem tuam a me? Sicut (Ex Augustino) non obliviscitur Deus, sic nec faciem (??)uam avertit. Sed more nostro Scriptura loquitur. Quasi nos obli- viscitur D(??)us, cum io ha(??) peregrinatione diu nos permittit laborare. Quasi fac(??)em suam avertit, cum a nobis manifestationem suae visionis abscondit.
passages.english: 2. How long, O Lord, will you forget me to the end? How long will you turn your face away from me? Just as (from Augustine) God does not forget, so neither does he turn away his face. But Scripture speaks in our manner. God as it were forgets us when he lets us toil for a long time in this pilgrimage. He as it were turns away his face when he hides from us the manifestation of the sight of himself.
passages.notes: 'mein finem' read as 'me in finem'.

passages.original: Ei statim se- q(??)tur : Timentes autem Dominum glorificat. Iste san- ctus qui ingreditur sine macula, qui potentes despi- cit, quia muli sunt : si quem vident timere Deum, licet pauper sit, tamen illum glorificat. Sicut (Ex Augustino) superiora pertinent ad perfectos, ita ea, quae nunc dicturus est, pertinent ad incipientes.
passages.english: And immediately there follows: But he glorifies those who fear the Lord. This holy man who enters without stain, who despises the powerful because they are wicked: if he sees anyone fearing God, even though he is poor, he nevertheless glorifies him. Just as (from Augustine) the preceding things pertain to the perfect, so the things he is now about to say pertain to beginners.
passages.notes: 'Ei' read as 'Et'; 'muli' read as 'mali' (wicked).

passages.original: 5. Vitam petiit a te. Resurrectionem (Ex Augustino) petiit, dicens, Pater, clarifica Filium tuum (Joan. 12. et 17.). Et tribuisti ei longitudinem dierum in soecu- lum et in soeculum soeculi. Idest longa tempora sae- culi hujus, quae haberet Ecclesia, et deinceps aeter- nitatem in saeculum saeculi.
passages.english: 5. He asked life of you. He asked (from Augustine) for resurrection, saying, Father, glorify your Son (John 12 and 17). And you gave him length of days for ever and ever. That is, the long ages of this world which the Church would have, and thereafter eternity for ever and ever.

passages.original: Ascribitur psalmus ipsi David media- tori, raani forti in persecutionibus, qui loquitur hic non tantum pro se, sed etiam pro martyribus suis, dirigenti in finem. Ecstasis, quae addi(??)a est in titulo, excessum (Ex Augustino) mentis significat : quae (??)it, vel pavore, vel ali- qua revelatione. Sed in hoc psalmo pavor maxime apparet perturbati populi Dei persecutione omnium gentium, et defectu per orbem fidei. Sed prior loquitur ipse mediator.
passages.english: The psalm is ascribed to David himself, the mediator, strong of hand in persecutions, who speaks here not only for himself but also for his martyrs, directing [them] to the end. Ecstasy, which has been added in the title, signifies (from Augustine) a going-out of the mind, which happens either through fear or through some revelation. But in this psalm it is above all the fear of the people of God that appears, troubled by the persecution of all the nations and by the failure of faith throughout the world. But first the mediator himself speaks.
passages.notes: 'raani forti' read as 'manu forti' (strong of hand, a play on the name David). 'dirigenti' is dative, agreeing with David/mediator; sense somewhat uncertain. 'quae (??)it' read as 'quae fit'.

passages.original: 9. Aperte autem de ipso sacramento vult dicere, qua fere(??)atur in manibus suis, cum subjungit : Gus- tate et videte, quoniam suavis est Dominus. Ostendit tibi (Ex Augustino, Enar. 2.) illam sanam insaniam, et sobriam ebrietatem illius David : qui in figura ne- scio, quid ostendebat, quando illi a miseri coram rege Achis dixerunt. Quomodo est (Ps. 110.)? Sic dicebat Dominus, Nisi quis manducaverit 149 carnem meam, et biberit sanguinem meum, non habebit in se vitam (Joan.
passages.english: 9. And he clearly means to speak of the sacrament itself, in which he was carried in his own hands, when he adds: Taste and see that the Lord is sweet. He shows you (from Augustine, Enarration 2) that sane madness and sober drunkenness of that David, who was showing I know not what in figure when those wretches said before King Achish: How is it? (Ps. 110). So the Lord said, Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in him (John
passages.notes: The citation 'Ps. 110' seems erroneous. 'a miseri' read as 'miseri'. 'fere(??)atur' read as 'ferebatur'. '149' is a page number, omitted. Breaks off mid-citation.

passages.original: Paulo ante soli- citi, et subito securi ex tribulationibus nimiis [Ant. nimis ], in magna tranquillitate positi. Nihil ti- mere, magna tranquillitas est in mente. Turbetur terra, turbetur mare, turbentur omnia elementa : Dei servus intrepidus manet. Mare autem (Ex Augustino) significat hoc seculum, in cujus 227 maris comparatione, tanquam terra videbatur gens Judaeorum. Non enim Idololatriae amaritudine tegebatur, sed erat tanquam arida, ipsa amaritudine Gentium tanquam mari circumdata.
passages.english: A little before anxious, and suddenly secure, placed in great calm after exceedingly many tribulations [another reading: exceedingly]. To fear nothing is great calm in the mind. Let the earth be troubled, let the sea be troubled, let all the elements be troubled: the servant of God remains fearless. Now the sea (from Augustine) signifies this world, in comparison with which sea the nation of the Jews seemed like land. For it was not covered by the bitterness of idolatry, but was like dry ground, surrounded by the very bitterness of the Gentiles as by a sea.
passages.notes: '227' is a page number, omitted.

passages.original: Per Sion montem ideo intelliguntur Judaei, quia sicut jam supra dictum est, ibi est ca- put regni. Filiae Judae non immerito accipiuntur Gentiles : sed propter confessionem 239 fidei. Ju- das enim confessio est : et omnes filiae : confessionis, filiae Judae sunt. Hinc (Ex Augustino) Apostolus ait : Non enim qui in manifesto Judaeus est, neque, quae in manifesto et in carne est circumcisio : sed qui in abscondito Judaeus est, et circumcisio cordis in spiritu non litera : cujus laus non ex hominibus, sed ex Deu est (Rom. 2.). Talis Judaeus esto : Glo- riare de circumcis one cordis. Admonentur alii, ut convertamur, cum subditur :
passages.english: By Mount Zion the Jews are understood, because, as has already been said above, there is the head of the kingdom. By the daughters of Judah the Gentiles are not wrongly understood, but on account of the confession of faith. For Judah means confession, and all daughters of confession are daughters of Judah. Hence (from Augustine) the Apostle says: For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not the letter; whose praise is not from men but from God (Rom. 2). Be such a Jew; glory in the circumcision of the heart. Others are admonished, that we be converted, when it is added:
passages.notes: '239' is a page number, omitted. 'Admonentur alii, ut convertamur' mixes persons; possibly corrupt.

passages.original: 3. Deus manifes e veniet : Deus noster, et non silebit. Prius occultus venit, infirmus in came appa(??)it. Erat gloriae species in divinitate, sed haec (??)alebat in hu- manitate. Si enim cognovissent, nunquam Dominum gloriae crucifixissent (1. Cor. 2.). Occultus ergo venit, ut judicaretur. Manifeste ve(??) et, ut judicet (Matth. 16.). Et hoc est (Ex Augustino), quod ait. Et non si- lebit. Silet modo a judicio, occultus in caelo. Patiens est super peccatores, non exercens iram, sed expec- tans poenitentiam. Tacui, inquit : nunquid semper tacebo? Et notandum, quod a(??)t Deus noster.
passages.english: 3. God will come openly, our God, and will not keep silent. First he came hidden; he appeared weak in the flesh. The beauty of glory was in the divinity, but this lay hidden in the humanity. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2). So he came hidden, to be judged; he will come openly, to judge (Matt. 16). And this is (from Augustine) what he says: And he will not keep silent. He is silent now from judgement, hidden in heaven. He is patient toward sinners, not exercising wrath but awaiting repentance. I have kept silent, he says; shall I always keep silent? And it should be noted that he says our God.
passages.notes: '(??)alebat' read as 'latebat'.

passages.original: 10.]) ei venenum, id est, peccata inde extrahere : ipsi nolentes veritatem obaudire, sed in fovea sua permanentes, ad veram lucem aspirare nolentes, alteram aurem cordis terrae, id est, prae- senti delectationi app nunt : alt(??)ram vero cauda ob- turant, id est, memo(??)ia praeteritarum delectationum. Non ideo (Ex Augustino) dicit Sapienter, ut incan- tationem laudet, sed ad similitudinem valet. Factum est hoc, et in primis temporibus fidei. Stephanus martyr praedicabat veritatem (Act. 6,), et tanquam tenebro(??)is mentibus, ut ea(??)in lucem ed(??)ceret, in- cantabat.
passages.english: 10]), its venom, that is, to draw out [their] sins from there: they, unwilling to listen to the truth, but remaining in their pit, unwilling to aspire to the true light, apply one ear of the heart to the earth, that is, to present pleasure, but block the other ear with the tail, that is, with the memory of past pleasures. He does not (from Augustine) say "wisely" in order to praise charming, but it serves as a comparison. This happened also in the first times of the faith. Stephen the martyr was preaching the truth (Acts 6), and he was charming, as it were, darkened minds, so as to lead them out into the light.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence, continuing from the context before ("they wish to draw them out of the pit ... and to kill what they are as sinners ... to draw out its venom"). Several scanning errors are read as evident: "app nunt" as apponunt ("apply"), "cauda" as caudā ("with the tail"), "memo(??)ia" as memoria, "tenebro(??)is" as tenebrosis, "ea(??)" as eas, and "ed(??)ceret" as educeret.

passages.original: 1. et 2. Sicut (Ex Augustino) solet Scriptura psalmorum mys- teria in titulis ponere, et trontem psalmi sublimitate sacra- menti decorare : ut Sciamus qui intraturi sumus, cum tam- quam super postem quid intus agatur legerimus, vel cujus domus sit, vel quisnam sit illius praedi(??) possesso : ita et in hoc psalmo scriptus est titulus de (??) ulo Habet enim, [Vers.
passages.english: 1 and 2. Just as (from Augustine) the Scripture of the psalms is accustomed to set mysteries in the titles, and to adorn the front of a psalm with the sublimity of a sacrament, so that we may know what we are about to enter, when we have read, as it were on the doorpost, what is done within, or whose house it is, or who the owner of that estate is: so also in this psalm a title has been written about a title. For it has, [Verse
passages.notes: The text breaks off at "[Vers."; the following context supplies the verse number and the psalm title. Scanning errors are read as evident: "trontem" as frontem ("front"), "praedi(??)" as praedii ("estate"), and "de (??) ulo" as de titulo ("about a title"), which is confirmed by "titulus de titulo" in the following context.

passages.original: 32. Et laus illa placebit Deo, super omne legale sa- crificium. Et hoc (Ex Augustino) ostendit per par- tem, cum suhjungit : Super vitulum novellum cornua producentem et ungulas. Talis enim quaerebatur vitu- lus in sacrificio, qui et novelius esset, et tam magnus tamen, ut cornua mitteret, aique ungulas fortes ha- beret.
passages.english: 32. And that praise will please God above every sacrifice of the Law. And (from Augustine) he shows this by a part, when he adds: "More than a young calf that puts forth horns and hoofs." For such a calf was sought in sacrifice, one that was both young and yet so large that it was putting out horns and had strong hoofs.
passages.notes: Scanning errors are read as evident: "suhjungit" as subjungit, "novelius" as novellus, and "aique" as atque. "By a part" (per partem) means that the psalmist names one particular sacrifice to stand for all sacrifice.
